rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands on the evidence instead of putting a blazer on inference. A's line, "Without a timeframe the number is bare and this angle is a topic, not a story," is exactly the discipline a founder needs before calling a reporter. B has real instincts, but "Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away" turns a supplied ownership fact into unsupported causation; that's how smart pitches get killed in paragraph two.
gaps_in_A: "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" overstates the physical setup. The update says customers can drop items off at stores, not that every store has a repair counter or in-store repair station.
"Story type: trend" is inflated for the retail-ops angle. This is a company operations/process story unless outside comparison proves a broader trend.

"Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" is a sharp headline, but it outruns the fact. The update says no new apparel line was announced, not that the stores have nothing new to sell.
gaps_in_B: "Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away" is the bad kind of clever. The update says Patagonia is privately held and directs profits to environmental causes; it does not prove causation, and only basic repairs are free.
"Most apparel reverse logistics is returns processing" and "operationally unusual" import market context that was not supplied. Maybe true, but you don't get to smuggle it in as fact.
"triages it into free/at-cost/resale" implies an operational connection between repair intake and resale routing that the update never states.
"The prevailing model in apparel is volume — growth comes from selling new units" is plausible business framing, but B presents it as settled proof instead of a claim that needs support.
